KEY MESSAGE 1...
In the mid/upper-levels, the synoptic pattern has changed little 
from 24 hours ago, with a large cyclone continuing to wobble over 
the Hudson Bay and a subtropical ridge that is slowly retrograding 
westward over the southern Rocky Mountains. The position of these 
two primary synoptic features has maintained a belt of intense flow 
over the CWA, with the 250 mb and 500 mb jet streaks objectively 
analyzed at 90 kt and 40 kt, respectively. A shortwave trough that 
previously detached from the western edge of the vertically-stacked 
low over the Hudson Bay continues to pivot towards the Adirondack 
and Catskill Mountains, which will maintain the belt of amplified, 
northwesterly flow over the CWA for the remainder of today. This 
will contribute to effective shear magnitudes near 45 kt, in 
addition to 60+ kt of shear throughout the cloud-bearing layer, 
supporting the potential for organized storm development along the 
southeastward-moving cold front as the airmass continues to recover 
in the wake of the morning MCS.

At the surface, a low was rotating onshore Lake Erie near ERI, with 
a warm front branching southward across southeastern OH and into 
southern WV. The cold front extends southwestward from the low 
towards CMH-IND along the I-70 corridor. A rapid, east-northeast 
progression of the warm front will occur over the next several hours 
as the shortwave trough digging into Upstate NY begins to become 
closed, which will aid in boundary-layer recovery as the low stratus 
deck begins to erode and southwesterly winds become slightly breezy 
within the pre-cold-frontal airmass. The resultant advection of 
already high theta-e air amidst pockets of differential diabatic 
heating within the cloud breaks will cause the boundary-layer to 
destabilize by 18Z as temperatures rise into the middle 80s, with 
rapid storm development expected along and ahead of the cold front 
within the weakly capped, pre-frontal airmass. SPC Mesoscale 
Analysis indicates a corridor of NCAPE of 0.2 nosing into areas 
along and southeast of the Ohio River, which corresponds to MLCAPE 
approaching 2,500 J/kg across the southern half of the CWA. 

The large CAPE values, combined with the aforementioned effective 
and cloud-layer shear magnitudes, will galvanize a risk for 
organized storms this afternoon and early evening as the cold front 
advances southeastward towards the Coal Fields. The orientation of 
the deep- and cloud-layer shear vectors will foster supercells 
embedded within broken, multi-cellular lines unzipping along the 
cold front. Right-moving supercells may become tornadic, and a 
tornado or two will be possible along and south of the I-64 corridor 
into the Coal Fields this afternoon. An attendant risk for damaging 
wind gusts between 50-60 mph and large hail up to half dollar size 
will also be possible with supercells, with the wind-damage risk 
focused near the rear-flank downdraft(s). Right-moving supercells 
are notorious for slowing in forward-speed and yielding a risk for 
flash flooding due to the extreme hydrometeor loading within the 
updrafts. Therefore, a localized risk for flash flooding will 
accompany any supercell(s), some of which may produce swaths of 
upper echelon rain rates that exceed 2"/hr. Mean wind vectors of 40 
kt will keep convection progressive otherwise. Elsewhere across the 
CWA, general showers and storms are forecast, with brief downpours 
possible as the cells move via advection across the central and 
northern portions of the CWA. Storm chances will wane following the 
passage of the cold front, with benign weather expected area-wide 
tonight into Wednesday morning, less the development of valley fog.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
The shortwave trough, accompanied by a closed low embedded within, 
will continue to progress slowly eastward over Upstate NY and New 
England through the end of the work week. Northwesterly flow on the 
backside of the trough will support a renewed potential for showers 
in the mountains Wednesday afternoon. Updrafts may struggle to reach 
heights high enough to produce lightning due to the depletion of 
CAPE and increasing subsidence aloft; however, lightning cannot be 
ruled out entirely across the mountains. Otherwise, a refreshing, 
northwesterly breeze is forecast area-wide Wednesday, with stratocu 
developing by late Wednesday morning. Dry and warm weather is 
forecast through Friday, with storm chances forecast to return this 
weekend due to a shortwave trough digging into the Upper Midwest as 
the subtropical ridge retrogrades over the Desert Southwest.
